source: Luchins (1942) Mechanization in problem solving: the effect of Einstellung (water-jar task), as reported in Bilalic 2008 and Binz & Schulz
finding: Founding paradigm. After five training problems solved by one long method (E-solution), people kept using it on critical problems that had a shorter solution, and many failed an extinction problem where only the short method worked.
numbers: Per Bilalic 2008: over 80% missed the shorter method on critical problems; 64% failed the extinction problem vs 5% of a control group without training (Luchins and Luchins 1959). Binz & Schulz: Luchins ran over 1000 people.
limits: Secondary report only; original thesis not opened. Water-jar numbers come from Luchins' tables, no individual data or reaction times.
agent_relevance: The model of the trap: a method that works gets reused, and the person does not notice a better one exists. Guardrail: after a first working answer, test for a shorter or different route only on a signal (G1), by running a check, not by feeling.

source: Binz, Schulz (2021 preprint) Reconstructing the Einstellung effect
finding: Reconstructed Luchins' thesis tables into data. Main experiment: with training, 128 of 155 used the E-solution on C1/C2 and 100 of 155 on C3/C4; the control group of 155 used it 0 times.
numbers: Plain 0.83 vs control 0.00 on C1/C2 (chi2=218.02, p<.001); 0.65 vs 0.00 on C3/C4; early test trials stronger than later (0.83 vs 0.65, chi2=13.00). N=310.
limits: Preprint, not peer reviewed at the time. Population-level counts only.
agent_relevance: A clean baseline: the effect is near total in the trained group and absent in the untrained control. Same task, same difficulty, so the cause is the earlier solution, not problem hardness.

source: Binz, Schulz (2021 preprint) Reconstructing the Einstellung effect
finding: Telling people 'Don't be blind' (pay attention to the problem) reduced the effect but did not remove it.
numbers: DBB group 87 of 153 used the E-solution on C1/C2 (0.57 vs 0.83 plain, chi2=24.16, p<.001); 57 of 153 on C3/C4 (0.37 vs 0.65).
limits: 1940s student samples; instruction wording matters.
agent_relevance: Warning-style prompts ('consider alternatives') help only partly. This fits G1 and the S3 design: do not rely on the model's own caution, change the process (fresh isolated attempts).

source: Binz, Schulz (2021 preprint) Reconstructing the Einstellung effect
finding: More training problems means a stronger set. Ten training problems gave a nearly complete effect; two gave a partial one.
numbers: 10 E-problems: 112 of 112 used E-solution on C1/C2 and 111 of 112 on C3/C4. 2 E-problems: 79 of 108 (0.73) and 59 of 108 (0.55). chi2=34.64 and 61.93, both p<.001.
limits: Different school-age samples than the main experiment.
agent_relevance: Dose-response: the more often one approach is shown in context, the harder it is to leave. For an LLM, many in-context examples of one method or repeated prior turns are the same dose. Keep exemplars varied.

source: Binz, Schulz (2021 preprint) Reconstructing the Einstellung effect
finding: Interleaving problems that need different solutions during training nearly removes the effect.
numbers: Alternating condition: 20 of 124 used E-solution on C1/C2 vs 97 of 121 in plain training (0.16 vs 0.80; chi2=100.65, p<.001). College students.
limits: Single study from the 1940s, not replicated here.
agent_relevance: Mixed, contrasting examples in a prompt may protect against set. Testable A/B for S3: blocked vs interleaved exemplars.

source: Binz, Schulz (2021 preprint) Reconstructing the Einstellung effect
finding: Time pressure increases the effect.
numbers: Speedy group 95 of 98 used E-solution on C1/C2 vs 126 of 153 plain (0.97 vs 0.82; chi2=12.08, p<.001); on C3/C4 94 of 98 vs 100 of 153 (0.99 vs 0.55).
limits: New York college and senior high school students.
agent_relevance: Tighter reasoning budgets should raise fixation. Consistent with G12: spend more where the first answer is cheap and likely wrong, not less. A cap (G11) must not remove the one alternative-generating step.

source: Binz, Schulz (2021 preprint) Reconstructing the Einstellung effect
finding: Resource-rational model: people turn prior preferences into a posterior policy that trades expected utility against decision cost. Three ingredients: prefer low physical effort, avoid costly computation (inverse temperature), adapt the prior to the environment (learning rate).
numbers: Simulation with learning rate 0.5 and inverse temperature 25: 90 of 100 agents used E-solutions on C1/C2 with training, 0 of 100 without. DBB simulated by raising attention (inverse temperature); time pressure simulated with inverse temperature 15. Ablation: removing any of the three ingredients fails at least one of Luchins' effects.
limits: Fit to 1940s aggregate data only; the model predicts reaction times, which were never measured. Not tested on chess or other domains.
agent_relevance: Gives a formal reading: fixation is a cheap, learned default, not a bug. An agent can model it as a prior over methods that updates with each success. A way to set thresholds for when extra search pays (G12).

source: Bilalic, McLeod, Gobet (2008) Inflexibility of experts - reality or myth? Quantifying the Einstellung effect in chess masters. Cognitive Psychology 56
finding: Experiment 1 (smothered mate problem). Strong players saw the familiar five-move smothered mate first, then looked for a shorter three-move mate. Only the strongest found it.
numbers: 2-solution problem, found the shorter mate: Grand Masters 100% (n=6), International Masters 50% (n=6), Masters 18% (n=11), Candidate Masters 0% (n=11). All who failed found the short mate in the 1-solution version (100%).
quote: only two of the Masters and none of the Candidate Masters found the optimal solution in the 2-solution problem
limits: One position. Players were told to find the shortest win with unlimited time and think-aloud.
agent_relevance: The signature result: knowing the pattern makes people stop at the first adequate answer. In S3 the first natural answer is the expected block.

source: Bilalic, McLeod, Gobet (2008) Inflexibility of experts - reality or myth? Quantifying the Einstellung effect in chess masters. Cognitive Psychology 56
finding: Quantified the cost: the familiar solution cut expert performance to that of players about three standard deviations weaker (about 600 Elo points).
numbers: IM 2-solution 50% vs Class A (2 SD above mean, n=8) 1-solution 63%; Masters 18% vs Class B 13%; Candidate Masters 0% vs Class C 0%. Logistic regression: 100 rating points down cut the odds of finding the short mate by a factor of 3.67 (B=.013, SE .005).
limits: Control is a different, weaker sample solving the version without the familiar line. Comparison across groups, not within person.
agent_relevance: A strong frame for our A/B: compare plain model on the trap item vs the same model on the same item with the familiar route removed.

source: Bilalic, McLeod, Gobet (2008) Inflexibility of experts - reality or myth? Quantifying the Einstellung effect in chess masters. Cognitive Psychology 56
finding: Experiment 2: five tactical positions, instruction 'find the best move' (more natural). Replicated the effect, smaller for stronger players.
numbers: Found the optimal move in the 2-solution problems: IM/GM 92%, Masters 69%, Candidate Masters 35% (n=12 each). Control, 1-solution version: Class A 91%, B 66%, C 47% (n=8 each). GEE logistic: 100 rating points down cut odds by 1.82 (B=.006, Z=3.72, p=.0002); predicted success .87 at Elo 2500, .67 at 2300, .37 at 2100.
limits: Positions partly from Saariluoma 1990; one easy problem (5) was solved by all experts so only weak players showed the effect.
agent_relevance: The block is a function of skill and item difficulty. A model's fixation will depend on how hard the better route is relative to its ability, not on the topic.

source: Bilalic, McLeod, Gobet (2008) Inflexibility of experts - reality or myth? Quantifying the Einstellung effect in chess masters. Cognitive Psychology 56
finding: Boundary: the effect needs an interaction of skill and difficulty. With an easy optimal solution, Candidate Masters were not fixated (all solved problem 5), while average players were. With hard problems even Grand Masters failed.
numbers: Problem 5: all experts solved the 2-solution version; Class C players showed the effect. Problem 3 (hardest): lowest scores even among super experts.
limits: Not a failed replication but a limit of the claim 'experts are blocked'.
agent_relevance: No fixed rule 'experts fixate'. Detect by item class: where the plain pass rate is mid-range and a familiar pattern exists (S0 gate).

source: Bilalic, McLeod, Gobet (2008) Inflexibility of experts - reality or myth? Quantifying the Einstellung effect in chess masters. Cognitive Psychology 56
finding: Experts did not know about the effect. 12 experts (mean Elo 2231) were shown both solutions and asked to predict success rates; they overestimated how many strong players would find the short route.
numbers: Exp 1 predictions: IM 86%, Master 74%, Candidate Master 59%; actual 50%, 18%, 0%. Exp 2 predictions 97%, 89%, 73%; actual 92%, 69%, 35%.
quote: You'll have to find a harder problem than this. No Master would miss [the shorter solution] in this position.
limits: Predictions made by experts of ordinary rank.
agent_relevance: Self-judgement of whether one would have missed a better route is poor. Supports G10 and G2: do not rely on the model's opinion that it explored enough.

source: Bilalic, McLeod, Gobet (2008) Inflexibility of experts - reality or myth? Quantifying the Einstellung effect in chess masters. Cognitive Psychology 56
finding: Not motivational: players who missed the better move searched as long as those who found it.
numbers: Exp 1 median search time: GMs 7 s, IMs 9 s, Masters 10 s before finding; those who failed searched 9, 8, 8 s. Exp 2: found vs not found, IM/GM 9.5 vs 9 s, Masters 12 vs 13 s, Candidate Masters 20 vs 22 s.
limits: Think-aloud may change behaviour.
agent_relevance: More thinking time on the same line is not the cure. Matches G11: extra tokens on one trace do not fix fixation; a different start does.

source: Bilalic, McLeod, Gobet (2008) Inflexibility of experts - reality or myth? Quantifying the Einstellung effect in chess masters. Cognitive Psychology 56
finding: Experiment 3: a rejected plan stays rejected. Players correctly dropped a standard plan in problem 2, then failed to reconsider it in problem 3, where other changes made it correct again.
numbers: 12 specialist players (5 GM, 4 Master, 3 Candidate Master). Only 1 of 5 GMs found the move; all others failed. Winners median Elo 2547 vs 2258 (Mann-Whitney U=2, p=.017).
limits: Small n. Players were specialists in that opening.
agent_relevance: A negative lesson from earlier in the context can block a later correct use of the same idea. For S3 history: log rejected ideas with the reason, and re-test them when the conditions change.

source: Saariluoma (1990) Apperception and restructuring in chess players' problem solving, as reported in Bilalic 2008
finding: First chess Einstellung studies using smothered mate. 10 of 12 failed to notice shorter solutions at first; in Exp 3 the familiar line blocked the optimal one.
numbers: Exp 3, two matched groups of 6: with the familiar solution present 11% of chosen answers were optimal and 67% the familiar one; with the familiar line disabled 69% found the optimal one.
limits: Secondary report via Bilalic 2008; no extinction control in the original design, so lack of knowledge was not fully excluded.
agent_relevance: Source of the control logic (disable the familiar route) that Bilalic quantified.

source: Bilalic, McLeod, Gobet (2008) Why good thoughts block better ones: the mechanism of the pernicious Einstellung (set) effect. Cognition 108
finding: Eye tracking explains the mechanism: players said they were hunting for a better move but kept looking at squares tied to the familiar solution.
numbers: Candidate Masters, 6 time intervals. 2-solution group (blocked): looking at smothered-mate squares did not change over time (interaction F(5,20)=0.6, ns). 1-solution control: gaze moved steadily to optimal-solution squares (F(5,20)=11.9, p<.001, partial eta2=.75). Control group found the short mate in 79 s (SD 25); blocked group declared smothered mate after 37 s (SD 20), then found the short mate in 148 s (SD 90) when shown the 1-solution version.
quote: The difficulty lies, not in the new ideas, but in escaping from the old ones
limits: Small groups (Exp 1 df=8, about 5 per group). 50 Hz eye tracker. Retrospective reports only.
agent_relevance: Mechanism: the first schema steers attention toward evidence that fits itself. For an LLM the analogue is attention and token probability going back to the same rationale. So new attempts must be isolated and seeded away from the first one (S3 fresh context).

source: Bilalic, McLeod, Gobet (2008) Why good thoughts block better ones: the mechanism of the pernicious Einstellung (set) effect. Cognition 108
finding: The effect lingers after the familiar option is removed, like a decaying prime.
numbers: Experiment 2: players who saw only the 1-solution problem solved it in about half the time of earlier-blocked players, t(44)=2.16, p=.036, d=.65. Experiment 1 comparison alone: 79 vs 148 s, t(8)=1.67, p=.13, d=1.2.
limits: Cross-experiment comparison, different players; interaction with skill n.s. (F(2,40)=0.9).
agent_relevance: After a failed fixated attempt, the same context is still contaminated. Reset context rather than 'try again' in the same thread (S3, S6).

source: Bilalic, McLeod, Gobet (2008) Why good thoughts block better ones: the mechanism of the pernicious Einstellung (set) effect. Cognition 108
finding: Theory: template theory / chunking (Gobet and Simon) links the effect to schema-driven attention. The first activated schema directs attention to schema-consistent features and so confirms itself. Authors tie this to confirmation bias and part-set cuing.
numbers: Competing accounts named: ACT-R production strength (Anderson and Lebiere), Instance Theory (Logan 1988), template theory. All can explain why stronger players find the optimal route (stronger or more differentiated trace).
limits: Models explain why skill helps, not directly tested against one another in these data. The discrimination-network implementation was not run for Einstellung.
agent_relevance: Gives a name to the S3 design: the first schema is a hypothesis that steers search. Counter it by forcing untried directions (code-held history) instead of asking the model to be open-minded.

source: Sheridan, Reingold (2013) The mechanisms and boundary conditions of the Einstellung effect in chess: evidence from eye movements. PLoS ONE 8(10) e75796
finding: Replicated and extended. 17 experts (mean CFC 2223) and 17 novices chose white's best move. When the familiar move was good but suboptimal, equal proportions of experts and novices chose it. When it was a blunder, the effect largely vanished.
numbers: Problem 1 (suboptimal Einstellung move Ba7): 8 of 17 experts and 8 of 17 novices chose it. Problems 2-4 (blunder moves): all experts and most novices avoided it. Time to first fixation on the target region: 407 ms experts vs 719 ms novices (t(32)=2.99).
limits: Only four problems, 12 trials per player. Boundary condition found: the effect needs the familiar move to be genuinely attractive.
agent_relevance: A fixation trap works only if the familiar answer scores well enough. For tests: use traps where the familiar answer is partly right (a blunder trap is too easy and tells nothing).

source: Sheridan, Reingold (2013) The mechanisms and boundary conditions of the Einstellung effect in chess: evidence from eye movements. PLoS ONE 8(10) e75796
finding: Eye data replicate the mechanism: experts who found the optimal move gradually looked away from the familiar region; those who chose the Einstellung move kept looking until the end.
numbers: Problem 1: experts who chose the optimal move (n=9) showed a declining linear trend in looking time at the target region (F(1,34)=43.45, p<.001); experts and novices who chose Ba7 showed none (F<1 and F(1,30)=1.76, p=.194). Blunder problems: both groups disengaged (experts F(1,66)=79.88, novices F(1,66)=10.84).
limits: Gaze is a proxy for attention; retrospective interviews: 2 experts and 4 novices who chose Ba7 did not rule out mate.
agent_relevance: The signal that separates success from failure is disengagement from the first line. In an agent, a measurable analogue: share of later attempts that restate the first approach (same candidate answer) as a fixation score.

source: Ellis, Reingold (2014) The Einstellung effect in anagram problem solving: evidence from eye movements. Frontiers in Psychology 5:679
finding: Same family of effect with letters: a familiar three-letter word in the middle of an anagram slowed solution compared with a nonword, but the accuracy difference was not significant.
numbers: 60 participants (df=59). Overall 52.7% correct, 4.2% wrong, 43.1% timed out. Word vs nonword: accuracy 51.7% vs 53.8% (n.s.); response time 15.3 vs 13.4 s (p<.01); dwells on central string 8.11 vs 6.76 (p<.001). Eyes spent longer on single letters in word trials.
limits: Effect shows in time, not in accuracy (a weak failure to replicate the accuracy cost). Task is not expert-based; familiarity both helps (encoding) and hurts (integration).
agent_relevance: Familiarity is a two-sided bet: it speeds encoding but slows recombination. A model that sees a stock phrase may parse it fast and miss a rearrangement.

source: Differences in the distribution of attention to trained procedure between finders and non-finders of the alternative procedure (water-jar eye tracking, Nagoya). Frontiers in Psychology 2022
finding: Modified water-jar task with eye tracking: those who later found the shorter procedure (C minus A) had already shifted gaze away from the trained procedure's jars two trials before they reported the finding.
numbers: 60 undergraduates, 46 analysed; 31 of 46 (67%) found the alternative before the last critical trial. Finders n=21 vs non-finders n=15 for gaze analysis. Gaze difference significant already at t-2 (F(1,34)=6.22, p=.018) and large at t (F(1,34)=87.16, eta2=0.72).
limits: Non-expert sample; 9 excluded for finding the alternative on the first critical trial. Author names not recorded from the text read.
agent_relevance: Disengagement precedes the insight, so it can be measured early. Agent analogue: attempts that move away from the first answer's evidence before a pass.

source: Greenberg, Reiner, Meiran (2012) 'Mind the trap': mindfulness practice reduces cognitive rigidity. PLoS ONE 7(5) e36206
finding: Experienced mindfulness meditators and a trained group showed lower Einstellung rigidity on a water-jar task. The alphabet-maze task showed no group difference.
numbers: Exp 1: meditators M=1.17 (SD 1.75) vs pre-meditators 2.93 (SD 2.02); t(25)=2.40, p=.01. Exp 2 after a mindfulness program: 2.19 (SD 2.09, n=27) vs waiting list 3.42 (SD 2.18, n=26), t(51)=2.11, p<.02. Alphabet-maze and water-jar rigidity correlated r=.10 (n.s.).
limits: One-tailed tests; small samples; the two rigidity tasks do not correlate, so rigidity is not one trait. Not an expertise study.
agent_relevance: Training of a general attention habit can lower the effect in people; for models the closest tool is the process, not exhortation (G1, G10).

source: Huang, Tang, Hu (2018) Unconditional perseveration of the short-term mental set in chunk decomposition. Frontiers in Psychology 9:2568
finding: Boundary conditions of a short-term set: in Chinese character decomposition, a set formed in minutes persisted even when the test problem looked unlike the practice problems (as the abstract describes it).
numbers: Base-set condition: one practice problem. Enhanced-set: 5-8 practice problems before the test. Experiment 1: test problem similar and 2-solution; Experiment 2: test problem differs. Abstract-level reading; no test statistics extracted.
limits: Abstract read; individual statistics not extracted. Chinese character task.
agent_relevance: A set built within one session may need no similarity cue to persist. In-context examples from the same prompt could fixate a model on unrelated items. To test.

source: Kim, Podlasek, Shidara, Liu, Alaa, Bernardo (2025) Limitations of large language models in clinical problem-solving arising from inflexible reasoning. Scientific Reports 15:39426
finding: mARC-QA builds Einstellung traps for LLMs: a familiar medical cue plus a decisive blocker that makes the stereotyped answer wrong. LLMs scored below physicians.
numbers: 100 hand-written USMLE-style items; 15 runs per model with chain of thought. Physicians (5) 66% (SE 5.3). Best models: DeepSeek-R1 52%, DeepSeek-V3 50%, Gemini 1.5 pro 50%, o1 48%; most models under 50%; some near 0% to 20%. Human-miss set (20 items): physicians 36% vs 73% on the rest; R1 51% on that set, confidently correct 45% and confidently incorrect 40%.
limits: Small benchmark written by the authors; physicians n=5; the link to Einstellung is by design, not measured as a time course. Models tested with cutoff Dec 2024.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM test of a familiar-pattern block. Overconfidence shown with consistency-based Brier scores (a G4 reminder that agreement is not proof).

source: Shidara, Prem, Kim, Podlasek, Liu, Alaa, Bernardo (2026) Advances in LLM reasoning enable flexibility in clinical problem-solving. AMIA Joint Summits Proc. (arXiv 2601.11866)
finding: Re-ran mARC on newer reasoning models: strong reasoning models avoided the traps about as often as physicians and did better than physicians on items humans mostly missed.
numbers: Top model Claude 4.1 Opus 75.1% (95% CI 73.8-76.3) vs physicians 66%; models not significantly different from physicians: Claude 4.1 Opus, Gemini 2.5-Pro, GPT-5.1, Grok-4-Fast-Reasoning. Human-miss subset (20 items): top 5 models 50-70% correct with high confidence; Opus 55% decisively correct, 25% decisively wrong, 20% indeterminate. 15 runs each.
limits: Same 100 items, now public, so contamination is possible; reasoning models improved over non-reasoning ones. Same small-n physician comparison.
agent_relevance: Fixation in LLMs falls with reasoning-trained models, so the trap size is model-dependent: measure it per model at S0 rather than assuming it.

source: Chen, Zhu, Huang, Wang (2026) MedEinst: benchmarking the Einstellung effect in medical LLMs through counterfactual differential diagnosis (arXiv 2601.06636)
finding: Paired control and trap cases isolate the effect: 5,383 pairs over 49 diseases; Bias Trap Rate is the share of control cases solved where the trap case is then missed. Frontier models have high base accuracy but severe trap rates.
numbers: 17 LLMs tested. Failure modes in reasoning LLMs: Blindness (key evidence not mentioned), Underthinking, Overthinking (rationalising a wrong prior). Text says GPT-5 has a disproportionately high Blindness rate. The multi-agent MDAgent lowered base accuracy from 40.26% to 29.70% versus its Qwen3-32B base.
limits: Only the abstract, introduction, metric definitions and discussion were read. The per-model table was garbled in extraction. The proposed ECR-Agent was not independently replicated.
agent_relevance: Counterfactual pairing (control vs trap) is the right test design for our A/B. Also: a multi-agent framework made it worse here, matching G9.

source: Alavi Naeini et al. (2023) Large Language Models are Fixated by Red Herrings: Only Connect Wall dataset (NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks; arXiv 2306.11167)
finding: Tests the fixation/Einstellung paradigm on LLMs with built-in red herrings from a quiz show (grouping 16 clues into 4 connected sets). The abstract states red herrings hurt model performance, and two synthetic sets (OCW-Randomized, OCW-WordNet) were built to test it.
numbers: Dataset split 62 train, 62 validation, 494 test walls. Static embedding baseline E5-base best among embeddings. The LLM results table was not extracted here.
limits: Only abstract, introduction and the start of results read; no LLM numbers extracted. Pointer for Angle B/C.
agent_relevance: A cheap, non-medical fixation benchmark with human reference scores.

source: Gu, Shi (2025) Diagnosing shortcut-induced rigidity in continual learning: the Einstellung Rigidity Index (arXiv 2510.00475)
finding: Borrows Einstellung for neural nets: a three-part index (adaptation delay, performance deficit, relative suboptimal feature reliance) for rigidity from a spurious cue in continual learning.
numbers: Two-phase CIFAR-100 with a magenta patch in phase 2; compared naive SGD, online EWC, DER++, GPM, DGR. CL methods reach accuracy thresholds earlier than a scratch baseline (negative AD) but end slightly lower on patched classes (positive PD); masking the patch helps CL methods, so the patch acted as a distractor.
limits: Abstract-level reading; the analogy to human Einstellung is loose, and the authors caution that results vary with backbone, dataset and cue salience.
agent_relevance: Shows a way to score rigidity: delay, deficit, reliance on the cue. Usable as a template for a fixation score in agent trials.
